Metabolomics Analysis: Data Pre-Processing and PCA

Member 1: Sergi Boluda Baldellou

Member 2: Mireia Fábregas Salazar

Member 3: Adrán Lopez i Albiol

Member 4: Maria Pascual Font

24 November 2026

This report documents the pre-processing, normality assessment and principal component analysis (PCA) of the metabolomics dataset from article 41598_2018_29592, comparing male and female samples.

0. Installing Packages and Project Setup

Packages, output folders and a helper that saves every figure as a vector SVG file.

library(readxl)
library(ggplot2)
library(mdatools)

## Output folders (relative to rmd/)
img_dir <- "../images"
res_dir <- "../results"
dir.create(img_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(res_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

## Helper: draws a plot straight into an SVG file (vector format, so it keeps
## the best possible resolution at any zoom level)
save_plot <- function(file, plot_expr, width = 8, height = 6) {
  svg(file, width = width, height = height)
  on.exit(dev.off())
  plot_expr
  invisible(file)
}

1. Data Pre-Processing

The raw Excel table is cleaned, transposed and converted to numeric, then checked for zeros and transformed.

1.1 Data Frame Creation

## Read table and delete columns from previous statistical analysis
df <- read_excel("../data/41598_2018_29592_MOESM2_ESM.xlsx")
df_clean <- df[, 15:ncol(df), drop = FALSE]
df_clean <- as.data.frame(df_clean)

row.names(df_clean) <- df_clean[[1]]
df_clean <- df_clean[, -1, drop = FALSE]

## Retrieve relevant metadata information (sex and label)
sample_labels <- as.character(unlist(df_clean["label", ]))
sex_chr <- as.character(unlist(df_clean["comment", ]))

## Delete rows from unnecessary metadata information
metabolomics <- df_clean[!rownames(df_clean) %in% c("mx class","mx sample", "comment",
                                                    "species","organ","treatment","label"), ]

## Transpose, rename rows and convert measures to numeric
metabolomics <- t(metabolomics)
metabolomics <- as.data.frame(metabolomics)
rownames(metabolomics) <- sample_labels
metabolomics[] <- lapply(metabolomics, function(x) {
  as.numeric(as.character(x))
})

## Add outcome variable (sex)
metabolomics$sex <- factor(sex_chr)
sex <- metabolomics$sex

## Save the clean data frame
saveRDS(metabolomics, file.path(res_dir, "metabolomics_clean_df.rds"))

1.2 Basic Exploration

# Only the first columns are shown, the table is very wide
head(metabolomics[, c(1:5, ncol(metabolomics))])
##        xylose xylonic acid isomer xylonic acid xylitol xanthine  sex
## M1_001  19537                 685          534    4766       37 Male
## M2_002   6619                 607           58    4525       28 Male
## M3_003  20015                1371          176    8679     1180 Male
## M4_004  13599                2057         1722   23461       85 Male
## M5_005  21525                1509          597    8231      729 Male
## M6_006  11649                1187          691    5288      834 Male
str(metabolomics, list.len = 5)
## 'data.frame':    121 obs. of  415 variables:
##  $ xylose                                                      : num  19537 6619 20015 13599 21525 ...
##  $ xylonic acid isomer                                         : num  685 607 1371 2057 1509 ...
##  $ xylonic acid                                                : num  534 58 176 1722 597 ...
##  $ xylitol                                                     : num  4766 4525 8679 23461 8231 ...
##  $ xanthine                                                    : num  37 28 1180 85 729 834 123 71 440 75 ...
##   [list output truncated]
table(metabolomics$sex)
## 
## Female   Male 
##     61     60
# Matrix with the metabolite measures only (outcome removed)
X <- metabolomics[, colnames(metabolomics) != "sex"]

The dataset contains 61 Female and 60 Male samples (121 in total). The text of the paper says 60 + 60, but its own Fig. 1A also shows 121 samples (e.g. X132_121), so all of them are kept.

1.3 Missing Values, Zeros and Log Transformation

We check for missing values and for zero or negative values, which would break the logarithm.

# Checking the data for missing values and zero/negatives (for the log)
sum(is.na(X))
## [1] 0
sum(X <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
## [1] 2
dim(X)
## [1] 121 414

There are two zero values. We locate them below (compound 109708 and creatinine).

# Check the values of compound 109708 and creatinine
idx <- which(X <= 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
zero_values <- data.frame(sample = rownames(X)[idx[, 1]],
                          metabolite = colnames(X)[idx[, 2]],
                          value = X[idx])
zero_values
##    sample metabolite value
## 1 F43_095 creatinine     0
## 2 F37_092     109708     0

These two values are the same ones found in the paper (page 4), where they were replaced by 1. Following the paper, we do the same before applying the log10 transformation.

# Replace zeros by 1 (as in the paper) and apply log10
X_fix <- X
X_fix[X_fix == 0] <- 1
Xlog <- log10(X_fix)

## Save the corrected and log-transformed matrices
saveRDS(X_fix, file.path(res_dir, "X_fix_zeros_replaced.rds"))
saveRDS(Xlog,  file.path(res_dir, "Xlog_log10_transformed.rds"))
write.csv(zero_values, file.path(res_dir, "zero_values_replaced.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

1.4 Descriptive Summary

# Summary
summ <- data.frame(
  mean   = sapply(X, mean),
  sd     = sapply(X, sd),
  median = sapply(X, median),
  skew   = sapply(X, function(x) mean(scale(x)^3))
)

head(summ)
##                           mean         sd median      skew
## xylose              37347.7190 44914.4303  25969  4.462174
## xylonic acid isomer  1627.9587   759.9815   1495  2.165127
## xylonic acid          482.6446   295.7584    381  1.486879
## xylitol             12139.1653 29025.0908   8075  8.305628
## xanthine              984.8099  3290.1289    614 10.217224
## valine               2735.4545  1983.2546   2283  1.744101
write.csv(summ, file.path(res_dir, "descriptive_summary_raw.csv"))

The metabolites are very skewed, which is another reason to apply the log transformation.

1.5 Gaussianity Assessment

We use the Shapiro-Wilk test and the skewness to see whether the log transformation improves normality.

# Gaussian distribution with Shapiro-Wilk test
shapiro_p <- function(M) sapply(M, function(x) shapiro.test(x)$p.value)
p_raw <- shapiro_p(X_fix)
p_log <- shapiro_p(Xlog)

c(raw_gaussian = mean(p_raw > 0.05),
  log_gaussian = mean(p_log > 0.05))
## raw_gaussian log_gaussian 
##    0.1207729    0.2222222

We obtain 12% Gaussian metabolites on the raw data and 22.2% after the log10 transformation, so 77.8% of the metabolites still fail the test. This is close to the 77% non-normal (~23% Gaussian) reported in the paper.

# Skewness before and after the transformation
skew_raw <- sapply(X_fix, function(x) mean(scale(x)^3))
skew_log <- sapply(Xlog,  function(x) mean(scale(x)^3))
c(median_abs_skew_raw = median(abs(skew_raw)),
  median_abs_skew_log = median(abs(skew_log)))
## median_abs_skew_raw median_abs_skew_log 
##           2.0032583           0.6934697
# Store the per-metabolite normality results
normality <- data.frame(shapiro_p_raw = p_raw, shapiro_p_log = p_log,
                        skew_raw = skew_raw, skew_log = skew_log)
write.csv(normality, file.path(res_dir, "normality_shapiro_skewness.csv"))

The log transformation reduces the median absolute skewness from ~2 to ~0.69.

1.6 Q-Q Plots

Q-Q plots of three example metabolites, before and after the transformation.

# Some Q-Q plot to see comparison (raw vs log10)
qq_file <- file.path(img_dir, "qq_plots_raw_vs_log10_xylitol_glucose_xylose.svg")
save_plot(qq_file, {
  par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  for (met in c("xylitol", "glucose", "xylose")) {
    qqnorm(X_fix[[met]], main = paste(met, "raw"));   qqline(X_fix[[met]])
    qqnorm(Xlog[[met]],  main = paste(met, "log10")); qqline(Xlog[[met]])
  }
}, width = 8, height = 9)
knitr::include_graphics(qq_file)

Normal Q-Q plots of xylitol, glucose and xylose: raw data (left) versus log10-transformed data (right).

2. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is applied to the log-transformed, centered and scaled data to explore the structure of the samples and the separation by sex.

2.1 Extreme Values per Sample

# Samples with the most extreme values (|z| > 3 on log data)
Z <- scale(Xlog)
extreme_counts <- sort(rowSums(abs(Z) > 3), decreasing = TRUE)
extreme_counts[1:10]
## M60_052 132_121 M31_024  F3_063  M2_002 M15_015 F47_098 F15_072 M10_010 M56_049 
##      85      41      34      34      16      14      14      12      10      10
write.csv(data.frame(sample = names(extreme_counts), n_extreme = extreme_counts),
          file.path(res_dir, "extreme_values_per_sample.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

2.2 PCA with prcomp

pca_base <- prcomp(Xlog, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
var_exp  <- pca_base$sdev^2 / sum(pca_base$sdev^2)
round(100 * var_exp[1:5], 2)
## [1] 19.68  5.93  5.71  4.64  3.31
saveRDS(pca_base, file.path(res_dir, "pca_prcomp.rds"))

PC1 explains 19.7% and PC2 5.9% of the variance (the paper reports 15.4% and 5.5%).

2.3 PCA Model (mdatools)

# PCA model
m <- pca(as.matrix(Xlog), ncomp = 8, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
saveRDS(m, file.path(res_dir, "pca_mdatools_model.rds"))

2.4 Variance Explained (Scree Plot)

# Scree plot: variance per component and cumulative variance
scree_file <- file.path(img_dir, "pca_scree_variance_and_cumulative_variance.svg")
save_plot(scree_file, {
  par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  plotVariance(m, type = "h", show.labels = TRUE, labels = "values",
               main = "Variance Explained")
  plotCumVariance(m, type = "b", show.labels = TRUE,
                  main = "Cumulative Variance")
}, width = 12, height = 5)
knitr::include_graphics(scree_file)

Variance explained by each principal component (left) and cumulative variance (right). 

cum <- cumsum(var_exp)
which(cum >= 0.50)[1]     # PCs for 50% of the variance
## [1] 10
which(cum >= 0.80)[1]     # PCs for 80% of the variance
## [1] 40
round(100 * cum[c(2, 5, 10)], 1)
## [1] 25.6 39.3 51.5
# Variance table of all components
var_table <- data.frame(PC = seq_along(var_exp),
                        variance_pct   = 100 * var_exp,
                        cumulative_pct = 100 * cum)
write.csv(var_table, file.path(res_dir, "pca_variance_table.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

10 PCs are needed for 50% of the variance and 40 PCs for 80%. The data is therefore not low-dimensional: after PC1 the variance decays slowly. A 2D score plot shows only about a quarter of the total variance, so a lack of sex separation there does not rule out separation in other directions. For this reason a supervised analysis (PLS-DA) could be used.

2.5 Score Plots

# Score plot
scores_file <- file.path(img_dir, "pca_scores_pc1_vs_pc2.svg")
save_plot(scores_file, {
  plotScores(m, comp = c(1, 2), show.labels = FALSE,
             main = "Scores PC1 vs PC2")
})
knitr::include_graphics(scores_file)

PCA scores on PC1 and PC2. 

# Score plot coloured by sex
scores_sex_file <- file.path(img_dir, "pca_scores_pc1_vs_pc2_coloured_by_sex.svg")
save_plot(scores_sex_file, {
  plotScores(m, comp = c(1, 2), cgroup = sex, show.labels = FALSE,
             main = "Scores coloured by sex")
})
knitr::include_graphics(scores_sex_file)

PCA scores on PC1 and PC2, coloured by sex. 

# With labels
scores_lab_file <- file.path(img_dir, "pca_scores_pc1_vs_pc2_with_sample_labels.svg")
save_plot(scores_lab_file, {
  plotScores(m, comp = c(1, 2), cgroup = sex, show.labels = TRUE,
             main = "Scores with sample labels")
}, width = 10, height = 8)
knitr::include_graphics(scores_lab_file)

PCA scores on PC1 and PC2, coloured by sex and labelled with the sample names.

2.6 Residuals

resid_file <- file.path(img_dir, "pca_residuals_5_components.svg")
save_plot(resid_file, {
  plotResiduals(m, ncomp = 5, show.labels = FALSE,
                main = "Residuals (5 PCs)")
})
knitr::include_graphics(resid_file)

Residuals of the PCA model with 5 components.
